utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and to those who are listening to the proceedings. Are there any matters to be raised? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. Mr. Thayer is back. I have had a chance to speak to him, and we will continue to speak on the topic of the closing of the Prosecution's case. I can tell you right now that we have decided that PW-055's 65 ter 133, we have decided to withdraw. There's roughly about five other witnesses that are either not speaking to us or are very sick or are those difficult issues but that we're going to have to turn up a bit more pressure on to try to get a commit. You may see us going for subpoenas, things like that. But we'll continue to talk this week and see if we can give you any more clear idea. And I started briefly with -- discussions with Mr. Gajic, since they have indicated there will be a 98 bis challenge. And in looking at any past practices, it's clearly in your discretion on how to do it. The Defence can either, as you -- can either go first and make arguments for whatever period of time, and then we can go, and then there can be a rebuttal or there doesn't have to be a rebuttal. So I'm looking to you for guidance on that, because ideally we would like to get that done that last week before the recess. I'm not sure it's going to be possible, but we do need -- and Mr. Gajic will be looking into how long he may need for that so that we can see if we can plan it. But we'll be looking for you on how that procedure will work. In any event, I just wanted to let you know that little bit of information, and we'll keep working on it so we can all plan the next couple of months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This was, indeed, the purpose of raising the matter last week. We are grateful for your information and the update we have received. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Greetings to everyone, to the President, to the Trial Chamber. And I would just briefly like to say something about our discussions with Mr. McCloskey on this issue. Unfortunately, the Defence at the moment cannot provide you with any more precise information. We are dealing with current witnesses, but we do not believe that we would be able to start with the 98 bis proceedings before the beginning of the summer break. There is a lot of material in this case. We still have to hear quite a few witnesses. And after we will have heard the main parts of their testimony, maybe we'll be able to give you some indication as to whether we'll be asking for 98 bis, how many witnesses we might have, and so on and so forth. We will definitely inform the Chamber as soon as we can. We are working on it. Of course, we have a few very demanding witnesses before us; Mr. Butler, Mr. Milovanovic. And I believe maybe a month or a month and a half before it is necessary to present argumentation in regard to Rule 98 bis we will be able to give you our position. This is our assessment, of course, which can change, but this is the best we can do at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you to you as well, Mr. Gajic. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just wanted to mention, one of the things I had mentioned to Mr. Gajic is the possibility of us, the Prosecution, doing their argument before the end of the -- before the recess started, even if there was a few witnesses that were left, because I'm sure a few witnesses left wouldn't make any major difference in a 98 bis argument. So I've discussed that with him, and I know he'll consider it, though I don't know if he'll want to go along with it, and that's perfectly understandable. So I just wanted you to know that was a possible option. Obviously, as you know, Mr. Thayer won't be with us afterward, and while I intend to take a major portion of that argument myself, I normally like to assign other key pieces to other people, Mr. Vanderpuye and Mr. Thayer, so ... And I would not expect the Prosecution to need more -- well, we would not need more than two days for such an argument, I can't imagine. Given the legal standard and the points of evidence that have been proven, I don't see us needing more than two days, just to give you an idea of what we're looking at, though. Of course, as we look closer, you know, I would like to have the freedom to revise that, but that's generally what we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your additional information. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I received an e-mail from the Prosecutor, where he's indicating or, rather, proposing that 98 bis argumentation should be presented before the end of the Prosecution case, but my position is that we cannot accept that. 98 bis argumentation should be presented after the presentation of the OTP case and before the Defence case, if necessary, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. First of all, we are looking forward to receiving an update in the next couple of days from the Prosecution about their position of withdrawing some witnesses, as you indicated, Mr. McCloskey. Secondly, the Chamber will consider the information we have received today by both parties, and we will for sure come back at a later stage and give some guidance as we understand the procedure in relation to 98 bis submissions. Thank you very much. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back to the courtroom. Again, I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Greetings to everyone here. May the peace reign in this house, and may God's will be done in these proceedings, and not mine. I would like to welcome Mr. Keserovic here and to apologise to him again for having to stay here in the Hague during the weekend. And here are my following questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Keserovic, we discussed document D64 just before we broke, and I would like to ask for this document to be put on the screens. It's D64, and it was in relation to something that Mr. McCloskey had asked us to clarify. I have a few questions for you in relation to this document that you can see on the screen before you. My first question is: Is this a document of the Drina Corps, its Intelligence Department, dated 12 July 1995, strictly confidential number 17/897? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can see that in the heading. It's a document of the Drina Corps. We cannot see the signature at the moment, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And the heading always tells us who prepared the document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to the rules of the Command and Staff War Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This document, in its entirety -- was it, in its entirety, forwarded after the Drina Corps received it from the Sector of Intelligence and Security Affairs?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, yes, could we please turn to the following page so that we can see the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, a small intervention. I think it's important for the understanding. 5 page, line 24 -- [In English] "Who prepared the document." [Interpretation] I think Mr. Tolimir said "who processed the document," not "who prepared the document."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Gajic. There's a huge difference between "processed" and "prepared."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But, Mr. Keserovic, thank you for waiting. You didn't have time to answer the question. We were interrupted. But my question to you was: This telegram that was received from the Main Staff, was it forwarded to all the units of the Drina Corps and all the users in its entirety? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was forwarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can one see from it that the telegram that had been sent from the Drina Corps, as we can see here, that it was received by the Drina Corps on the 20th of June at 2150?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we see that it was received on the 12th of July at 2200?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And can we see that it was sent or forwarded to the end user at 2210?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we also see on this last page that the document had already been filed in the subordinated units, as we can see here in the stamp, Command of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, the 13th of July? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. The date was wrong on line 25 on what I'm looking at. It's June. And it's an important document, so I think we should get that right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, that was part of your question. You should verify what you are talking about. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. It's also -- it says "20th of June," and this is, I think everyone agrees, a 12th of July document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Keserovic, can we see on the document "12th of July, 1995" and the time of receipt and the time of processing and the time of the forwarding of the document to the subordinated units? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All three terms are listed in there, "Received" and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the document moved so that the signature is visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, the person who processed this telegram, did he put under the text the function and the name "General Major Zdravko Tolimir"; is that correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one who processes the document put only one part of your function, just "Chief," believing or counting on something that we cannot see here in the decoded document, that this would imply the chief of the Sector for Intelligence Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When the person who has processed the telegram signs it with his superior officer's name, why would he do that and what are his intentions? Can you tell the Chamber that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often the intention is to get the units to carry out the tasks with more seriousness, and also there are some intelligence information that units of lower level couldn't have obtained using their own sources and it is, therefore, necessary to point out that the information contained had been gathered at the highest level. And they transfer the order using the authority of the chief of sector at the top level, at the top level of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have in the e-court the first page of the document so that I can put a different question. He probably needs to see it because since the last time we were together he may have forgotten the content. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, the person who processed this document, did he -- in addition to sending it to all security organs of the Drina Corps, did he send it also to General Krstic at the forward command post at Pribicevac and Colonel Popovic to the forward command post in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the commander of the corps and all the levels above him are persons or officers who are originally being briefed about all the documents issued by the Security Service. In other words, the command structures need to be made aware of the requests made in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Please, on the basis of the parameters that we have seen while reading the telegram, can we conclude that this document was available to all the intelligence organs within the corps and commanders of the operation that was being carried out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was available to all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Later on, when you arrived in the zone of the corps between the 17th and the 18th, did you find out whether the proposal that's contained in the telegram was acted upon? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure I have fully understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, let me put it differently. Upon your arrival to the Drina Corps's zone after the fact, on the 7th -- on the 17th of July, did you find out from the organs in the Nova Kasaba that they were carrying out the registration process according to the orders by the security organs or the Security Administration? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the Military Police Battalion, Malinic, told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Malinic tell you who issued him this order and what else was going on in Nova Kasaba on that day? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Malinic told me that Colonel Beara had forwarded the order. I'm not sure how. I think it was via the duty officer of the unit. And the order was that Nova Kasaba Stadium was to be location where the POWs would be gathered and where they would be registered, including all the basic data on them. He also told me that the process that was well underway had been interrupted and suspended, stopped, by General Mladic, the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did Mladic interrupt or stop this for the purpose of addressing the POWs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Malinic stopped, after he was told to do so by the commander of the Main Staff, to register the POWs. In the meantime, General Mladic addressed the POWs. I'm not sure that I know whether Mladic issued any further orders to Malinic, but I do know that as of that moment, and maybe even before that, Malinic was active in blocking the road between Kasaba and Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Malinic tell you that journalists also came to the Nova Kasaba football field to take footage of the POWs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him telling me anything about the journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he tell you that immediately after the address by General Mladic he took the POWs immediately, as ordered, to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I already said that. Immediately after that, means of transportation, mainly buses, came to the area of Nova Kasaba. As far as I remember, it was mainly buses, and the POWs were transported in a convoy to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that on the 13th, in Nova Kasaba, POWs were being registered until the moment they were transferred to Bratunac? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one can put it like that, until the arrival of the commander of the Main Staff, and then they were loaded onto the buses and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see D152 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to stop you for a moment. Before we leave this document, I would like to put a question to the witness. I need some clarification because I'm slightly confused. Can you help me. In the headline, I see "Command of the Drina Corps, Intelligence Department." Who was the head of the Intelligence Department of the Command of the Drina Corps in mid-July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Drina Corps Command, according to what I know, and I think that it was so, did not have an intelligence department. It had an intelligence/security affairs department which comprised both of those functions. That's how it was in most of the corps, including the Drina Corps. The chief of the Security/Intelligence Affairs was Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, and the Intelligence Department, I'm not sure, but included at that time Major or Lieutenant-Colonel Pajic. I think so. I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we all agree that Mr. Tolimir was not a member of the Command of the Drina Corps but of the Main Staff. Was it customary that a member of the Main Staff would sign a document sent out by the Command of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. And there is just one thing. For some reason, in order to speed up the process technically, so it's a technical matter that the heading was changed, while the contents stayed the same. There are technical omissions here, so that, in any case, General Tolimir should not have and did not sign documents of the Drina Corps Intelligence/Security Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it possible, taking into account your statement that the content remained the same, that there was a command, an order, from the Main Staff to the Drina Corps which was in this way forwarded to a lower level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the way I understood the document is like this: There is an original document - it should exist - from the chief of the Sector for Intelligence and Security Affairs of the Main Staff, General Tolimir, which came to the departments of the Sarajevo Romanija and the Eastern Bosnia Corps, as we can see here, and that document was just passed along by the department of the Drina Corps to their subordinate units without processing it analytically, without creating a new document. They just, roughly speaking, cut and pasted it and sent it as such. So there is just one document. There are differences there. There is one document from the Main Staff, from General Tolimir, and there is this one from the Drina Corps, but the contents of both are identical. That was simply the practice in order to speed up this process of informing everybody about the tasks. This is how we used to do it in practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this explanation. Would you agree that a person who has no information about the structure and the persons involved would form -- could form the impression that Mr. Tolimir was the chief of the Command of the Drina Corps Intelligence Department, if you combine the heading and the signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, one could conclude that from this, with the proviso that there is a memorandum at the bottom, the square one, containing the processing times, the time of receipt and of distribution, so this would then possibly indicate that the document did not originate from the person who was in the heading. But, generally, if you just looked at it, you would probably draw the same conclusion that you did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Keserovic, do you know if, in the practice of the Intelligence/Security Sector's work, a general would negate or deny anything that was written by their subordinates, pursuant to the law, or would he always accept that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware that you ever disputed something by your subordinates in relation to any assignment that you issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keserovic. I had to ask you this in order to avoid any dilemmas. I wouldn't want anybody to think that I was saying that this was not my document. I did not deny that any documents were mine, issued in wartime, just like you said now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at D152, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document shouldn't be broadcast because it's confidential.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Keserovic, we're not going to read out the first and last name. This is a protected witness. You're looking at the statement of a witness, and later on we will see. But can we now look at page 3, please, paragraph 1 on that page. Thank you. Perhaps it would be even better to look at page 2, the last line in that sentence. I'm going to read the sentence beginning on page 1: "Some were taken to a special, separate group on the pitch, and we were all sitting," the witness said, "for about an hour after I arrived. General Ratko Mladic came." So he arrived, and then we will look at the jeep -- if you look at the next page, maybe we can scroll down. "He arrived in the jeep, and I think that he was in uniform. I knew this was Mladic because I recognised him, and I was told that he would come. I was some 10 to 15 metres away from him when he gave a speech, standing at the side of the pitch. He spoke without a loud-speaker, quite normally, because it was very quiet. He said that he was General Mladic and that we would all be exchanged, that there were hundreds of Serb lines between here and Tuzla and that not even a bird would be able to get through those lines. He said we would be organised into groups to collect all the bodies from the hills, and then we would be taken to Bratunac to have lunch there. He then chose five of his men to begin making lists of our first and last names, which took almost an hour." Please, based on what this witness says about the 13th, when he was captured, can you see from this that General Ratko Mladic, the commander of the Main Staff, registered all those who were prisoners of war and that he ordered a subordinate of his to do that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information about General Mladic saying or, rather, organising that all the names be taken is not something that I had. Malinic never told me anything about it. This is the first time that I'm hearing about it. But it's evident from this statement that this did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of this statement by this Prosecution witness, a person from the B&H Army, does that indicate that General Mladic wanted to record as large a number of prisoners of war as possible on the 13th, just as this witness here is talking about, precisely the 13th? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to speculate about the motives of General Mladic, whether he wanted to show that there was a larger or a smaller number of them. But if he wanted to have them registered, I assume that the idea was to show the precise number of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right, please. Thank you. These activities regarding the registering of prisoners of war, do they, de facto, coincide with the measures that were ordered, in the instructions that we were just looking at, to register as high a number as possible to avoid manipulation about the fact that Srebrenica was, in fact, a demilitarised zone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the context, that does seem to be the same goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 18 of the transcript of the 9th, I think -- I apologise for not preparing that earlier. That is the transcript of the 10th. Then on page 18, line 21, you were asked by the Prosecutor if we had the escort of prisoners is any category, and you answered, on page 21, line 18, that "escorting" refers to all categories of persons that needed to be transferred from one location to another, which means that this could also apply to prisoners of war. Now I'm putting a question to you because of the transcript. Because in the English "sprovodjenje" is being interpreted as "escorting." Can you please tell us whether "sprovodjenje" means transfer of persons, materiel, and equipment from one place to another for the purpose of their security, the security of the road that they are using, and so on and so forth? Is this a more complex action that encompasses also security of the transport and the vehicles that are part of the transport? Thank you. Can you please explain that, as an expert? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely that. When someone who is responsible for personnel, for equipment, and for prisoners of war, and it could also be some other persons who were interesting, from the security point of view, decides that they need to be transferred, then the military police unit would provide personnel who would provide security for this transport on that particular road, regardless of the manner in which they were being transferred. They could be secured while walking or using vehicles of any type. There are different types of escort activities. It could be a motorised escort. They could be walking on foot. There could be a direct one, as was the case here, within -- inside the vehicles. So different modalities are possible. In any event, this is a complex action whereby the unit carrying out the transport undertakes the responsibility for the security of persons and equipment on that particular section of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keserovic. You also, on this page, on page 19 of the transcript of the 10th, in line 1, were asked: "Would the security organs need to inform the commander, as far as prisoners of war are concerned?" Because the question refers to that. So my question is this: Would the security organs first of all find out from the commander first that a transport needed to be carried out and after that they would need to report back to him and not inform him about how this particular task was done? Could you please explain this to us? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's like you said. The security organs would find out from the commander about the assignment, and then they would report back to him after the assignment was carried out. And then the informing would go from the superior to the subordinate, and the reporting back goes from the subordinate to the superior. That is the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When, in this specific case, the prisoners of war were transferred from the pitch to Konjevic Polje, did the police first receive information about it and then proceed to carry out the transfer from that location to the destination where they were supposed to be transported?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were issued the assignment by General Mladic, the authorised official, the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. On page 34 of the transcript of the 11th of May of this year, you are talking about what Malinic told you when, on the 17th of July, 1995, you arrived at Nova Kasaba, and that that was the first time that he informed you that there were prisoners of war in Kasaba, some 2- to 3.000 of them, and that it was his task to register them all and transfer them from Nova Kasaba to Bratunac. Was that how it happened, and are you -- do you want to add something to it if I perhaps missed something? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the transcript, we're talking about page 13966.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Keserovic, what is your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is that this is, in essence, what Major Malovic [as interpreted] informed me about and what General Tolimir said just now is actually what I stated a number of times in my testimony so far. This is my best recollection of that particular matter from that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keserovic. I asked you this because you are finding out for the first time from Malinic about the number of people and the location. I'm asking you this; my question is this: Did he then tell you 2- to 3.000, and was that why you were not able to be so precise about it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he said between 2- to 3.000, because he did not register all of them, he did not complete the definite list at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Keserovic, are you aware that Mr. Momir Nikolic, on the 11th of April of this year, on page 76, lines 17 to 19, said, more or less, that that was the number of prisoners of war who were accommodated in Bratunac? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have occasion to see Mr. Nikolic's testimony. I'm not familiar with what he said and whether he confirmed it or whether the numbers tally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Because you were unable to see that before, I wanted to quote a part of the transcript from that testimony of the 11th of April, page 76, lines 17 through 19. Mr. Fluegge, the Presiding Judge, asked the following: "How many people died in the column, having in mind the column breaking through from Srebrenica via Baljkovica to Kladanj?" Nikolic responded by saying: "In my estimate, between 3- and 4.000 people from the column lost their lives, but I really don't know any more than that, and it would make no sense for me to speculate." That is what he said. When Judge Nyambe asked him how he came up with the assessment of 92 per cent of those who were killed, at page 79, lines 3 through 10, he said: "The basis for my assessment is the knowledge I have about the number of people who were separated in Potocari, I'm also discussing assessments here as well. I saw many people who were taken prisoner throughout the period in question on the spot, and en route from Srebrenica to Konjevic Polje, and onwards from Konjevic Polje. I base my estimate on that information. I counted the people who were separated in Potocari. I also know how many were taken prisoner and temporarily accommodated in Bratunac and Kravica." My question is this: Did you know already or do you hear for the first time that Nikolic actually counted the people he had in those locations, as he answered to Judge Nyambe? In other words, there is a piece of information indicating how many people there were in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until now, I really had no occasion to know that Nikolic counted them. The information he provides is something that I was not aware of; not in that sense, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Momir Nikolic, in his testimony and in his statement, which is number 7280, at page 12, line 6, he said that on the 12th and the 13th there were between 600 and 650 people. Then in line 15 at page 74, he said -- it's actually lines 13 through 15, he said: "I have in mind the 400 prisoners in Konjevic Polje." My question is this: Did you know that Nikolic separated only 650 men in Bratunac when he separated the able-bodied men from the rest and that he said that he knew of only 400 prisoners in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what Momir Nikolic was doing at the time. I hear of this information for the first time, and it's difficult for me to address it in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The basis of my objection was his answer, because this could go on forever. This has never been part of his testimony, Momir Nikolic. It has nothing to do with Nova Kasaba or Malinic, in this sense. And the numbers that he's picking out, it's difficulties to say where he's even getting these. So this -- I would object to this kind of confusing, calling-for-speculation sort of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the questions about numbers are rarely seen through the prism of witness statements and other documents by the Prosecution. I don't know why that is so. I'm asking this of the witness because the RS government also drafted a report in which they approximated the figure of those killed at 8.000. If we don't have specific data, how can the RS government have it? I'm asking the witness about this because at the time he was a member of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have every right to ask questions about the knowledge of this witness about numbers of victims, about numbers of separated men. But now you are putting the evidence of another witness to him, and he told us very clearly he really had no occasion to know that Nikolic counted them. This witness told us that he doesn't know anything about the testimony of the witness Nikolic. Therefore, you should ask him about his knowledge and not about the testimony of another witness. That would be much more helpful. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I believe it is in the interests of all of us to come up with a figure which can be presented to the public. The witness did not deny what Mr. Nikolic said. He just simply stated that he wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Keserovic, do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is the reason why I asked you to ask the witness about his knowledge. He clearly indicated that he doesn't know anything about the testimony of Mr. Nikolic. Please put questions to the witness about his knowledge. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I was just about to ask him about his knowledge when I was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Keserovic, do you know what the RS government based their figures on, because you were in the RS at the time? What were the sources, what was the information they relied on when they included the figure of 8.000 people killed in Srebrenica? Did they rely on some documentation that we may find useful?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I worked for the Ministry of Defence, and I believe I've answered this already, I did have some knowledge as it existed within the Ministry of Defence and the VRS. That information was provided to the commission. They seemed to be dissatisfied with these initial figures and information, which stopped at several thousand, and the Office of the High Representative in Bosnia-Herzegovina reacted to it. They removed the commission president from his post and replaced some of the members. Then they issued them some tasks. I left the position shortly afterwards, and I was no longer informed of the events. What I do have, in terms of information from the time, which I gained through discussions with different people, is that the figure was arrived at by Mr. Smail Cekic on the Bosnian side. He took some of their information, as well as certain lists, and put them in the report. And then the government, under a certain amount of pressure, had to accept that as its own report. That is what I heard. Whether indeed it was true, I don't know. There may have been all sorts of things involved. But simply put, the government did not, at the time, have valid documentation which could provide specific figures. Another thing about the report. There was something else which indicates the lack of seriousness and professionalism in the work surrounding it. There was a list of participants in the Krivaja operation in 1995, and that list comprises some 23- or 24.000 names, which is basically science fiction. They simply collected all war lists, the so-called VOG-8, starting with all units from the Drina Corps down, and they merged it all together, coming up with that number. The situation one worked in at the time did not allow for a professional approach to the matter to be completed. This is what I know from the relevant period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keserovic. We showed you D176. I would kindly ask that it be shown in e-court again so that we could see that the figures we have been referring to in the course of your testimony have been covered up or doctored. Could we have page 5 of the document. Let us look at the last paragraph, the last sentence on the page: "According to our rough estimate and information, the corridor up to now" -- Let's now flip the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please provide us with the relevant -- the number of the relevant paragraph in English as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It is the next page in the English version, the last paragraph on page 5 in the Serbian. This sentence begins with: "The 22nd of July, 1995 ..." Aleksandar, could you be of assistance and tell us what the page is in English? It is page 9 in English. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 22nd of July, 1995. I don't seem to have the right page now. Could we please have the last page, where I started reading, beginning with: "According to our rough estimate ..." Thank you. I apologise. Something seems to be wrong with the hardware, and I don't read English. I started reading a sentence which lacks its end. We don't see the rough estimate figure. Perhaps there is a figure in the English text, but not in the Serbian, in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it's a question of your preparation of the examination, not of the hardware or the software. The documents are on the screen, and you just should give the right number of the pages and the paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would kindly ask the e-court to assist. I specified the page. Perhaps they can find the corresponding pages in both languages. There is no other way for me to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please give us the page number in B/C/S first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S, it's page 5, and page 7 in English, as far as I can see. Page 7, bullet point 5 in English. We can see it in Serbian. It's the last sentence. I quote: "In our rough estimate and in information, the corridor was up to now used by ..." And then we have something missing when the document was copied, photocopied. Therefore, we can't see how many people actually used the corridor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Mr. Keserovic, do you know why the Muslims were covering up or hiding the exact figures of people who crossed the territory of the RS via Baljkovica when they used the corridor en route to Nezuk and Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. There's no factual foundations for that assertion at all, and certainly not from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it. I mean, he should have a foundation for any fact in a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, indeed, you said: "Do you know why the Muslims were covering up or hiding the exact figures of people?" Please give a reference for this statement included in your question. Or rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I put the question on the basis of this document. Everything in the document has been translated except for the number of people who had passed through the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And this is my question: If the Muslims tried to hide that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tolimir. That's not correct. It was everything translated. You can see it. The last line in B/C/S ends because there was not a proper -- there is not a proper copy. In the English, you see: "According to a rough estimate and our intelligence, a total number of ..." And then the text is missing. It's exactly the same. It's not a translation issue. Why do you put the question that the Muslims were hiding a number of people? It's not in here, in this document. This sentence says something different. It's not very precise, but it's something different. Put a question to the witness, but rephrase it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Keserovic, do you know how many Muslims passed through the corridor, and is it something that any of the fighting factions ever published?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have an opportunity to hear different estimates. However, not one of them was precise or reliable. Initially, the estimates were just derived, although the number of inhabitants of the enclave was not known. And using that as the basis, the figures concerning the column were between seven or eight on one end and maybe up to 15.000 people who were involved in the break-through. I don't know which of the numbers are more or less reliable, but I did not hear any really relevant and reliable data.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keserovic. Since it was not known, how many people set off from Srebrenica, is it or was it possible to find out how many of them arrived at Nezuk?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon their arrival in the territory of Tuzla or the zone of the 2nd Corps of the BH army, it was possible to determine the number of people who got out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keserovic. Among people who are doing research on the issue in Republika Srpska, is there any view on why was it never determined how many people actually left and how many people arrived after passing through the corridor, and why was it that the Muslim authorities never published any data on it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that the views on various data are very different. There are different assessments, different interests, and there's too much unclear about what was going on during the conflict, about what the nature of the conflict was, and many other things. Each of the sides has its own truth, and these truths cannot be reconciled. And it is, therefore, very difficult to use the data in any serious assessment or conclusion-making process.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keserovic. If you would know the number of -- exact number of people who managed to get out because they were registered, they received later some financial aid, would all that help avoid future problems and inconsistencies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most probably.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, can we please have D151 on the screen, but it must not be broadcast to the public because it's a document that came in through a protected witness. We should also not read out any data on the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And after you've seen the first page, I'd like to move immediately to the following page, where we can find the text that I want to ask you about. Thank you. We will read the third paragraph on this page. It starts with the words: "As we were breaking through from this area in the same direction in which the first group of our people went, we encountered warnings or markings which stated -- or signs saying 'Mined.' I assumed that our people who had passed earlier through these areas left those signs. From there, we headed towards Pobudjska Kamenica, where we met with part of the first group, but the Chetniks surrounded us there and opened fire on us, killing over 300 people and wounding a large number. We were in disarray." And that's the end of quote. This is my question to you: Did you have an opportunity to hear that there were losses or casualties in the Muslim column while they were trying to make their break-through from Srebrenica towards Nezuk via Baljkovica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a later stage, there was information that there were a lot of casualties in the fighting. There was also information which I'm not closely informed about but that there were suicides by hanging or shooting at oneself en route. So on the route to Tuzla, and especially during the last conflicts with the Zvornik Brigade, that they did have casualties, but the number -- what the number is exactly, I wouldn't know. But when you're making a break-through, when you're trying to get out of an area where you're surrounded, well, one must expect a lot of casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether Muslims ever made public any information about the number of casualties during the break-through from Srebrenica to Nezuk via Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that casualties, such like these that were casualties of the fighting, that they're included in the number of victims who were summarily killed in various reports?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is obviously something wrong with the figures. During the last year or two, efforts are being made to make a classification of even those people who had been buried in the Memorial Centre in Potocari, because some killed who had been buried there actually fell in various other conflicts throughout the 1992-to-1995 period, even those who simply died of natural causes, or people who died somewhere else, on some other battle-front but who were from the area of Srebrenica. When will all this be cleared up? I don't know. But the process is underway slowly. But something is happening. And there is information, clear information, that the victims of Srebrenica, the alleged victims of Srebrenica, include various people who may have died in many different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please see 1D100, page 7 in e-court, lines 10 to 17.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is entered into evidence as Exhibit D166. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. While this document is coming up, I would like to put a question to the witness. In your last answer, you told us about efforts to find out the realistic number of victims, and you gave us your opinion about those buried in the memorial in Potocari. What is the basis of your information that there were people buried who died of natural causes, at least not as a result of the killings? What is your source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My source is public information that the committee, joint committee, for the search of the missing from the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina is submitting to the public, and they did confirm. So this is the information provided by the committee dealing with these issues. And according to them there are people who were not killed in July or were not killed there, but that for certain ethical reasons, and this is something that different -- both sides in the committee, members from both sides confirm, that for ethical reasons people were buried there because they were from there or because their families asked that. In other words, I have this information at my disposal based on what the committee for the search of the missing is publishing. And the state organs, I must add, are imposing upon them, and all the others who are dealing with this issue, to complete the investigation. It was also something that was discussed in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the Council of Ministers of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Requests were sent to leaderships of various entities, of the two entities there. In other words, this is a story that is very topical in Bosnia for the last year or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You just said "my source is public information." Did you have the opportunity to read this report from the joint committee or did you get the information by the media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostly from the media. And I rely mostly to information that was stated at assemblies of -- at the meetings of the Assembly, where various officials present such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to read the report itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue. There is some minutes left before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, before you, you can see a report by a witness who testified here on the 14th of March, 2000 [as interpreted]. The witness's name is Jean-Rene Ruez, and he said this area was processed in 1996 by a team of experts from Finland who worked there in 1996: "It was unrelated to our activities. They collected the remains, but one must add that 600 bodies were found in the area, bodies of victims that were killed during fighting, in ambush actions, during shelling, and possibly through other types of events that are difficult to explain. It is difficult to determine whether it was a situation where fighting was involved or something else." And this is my question to you: Do you know that the 600 victims in question are -- both by the OTP and by the commissions in Bosnia and Herzegovina, are treating the 600 as people who were summarily executed, although Mr. Ruez here tells us that they were killed in fighting? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already spoke about that. I believe that there were no attempts to differentiate between the conditions under which people were killed or died, that everyone was put into the category of victims, according, at least, to information by the Government and the leadership of Republika Srpska and its commissions. That's the only information that I basically have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First of all, the witness, Ruez, was not interrogated in the year 2000, but 2010, on the 14th of March, just at the beginning of this trial. Just a correction to the record, page 32, line 11. Then you have the floor, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I object to this statement with no -- there's no legal -- there's no factual foundation that it's the OTP's position that people in these woods were killed in summary executions. In fact, it's the OTP's position, as it's been clearly stated in Mr. Janc's testimony, that there were -- I can't remember the exact numbers, but it's up to 800, 900 surface remains found in that area, and it's -- our position is precisely what Mr. Ruez's position was. It's very difficult to determine if those people were murdered, died in combat, died of shelling, how they were killed. So when he says the OTP has suggested these were summary executions, he's wrong. And unless he can cite some sort of place where that is said, you know, he should get his facts right. And I believe I probably stood up over the months here and said that we do not contest that there is at least a thousand surface remains in this area, that it's unclear how they died. That has the position ever since Mr. Ruez first said it, I think, in the Krstic case. So this fantasy should stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should reconsider your position about the position of the OTP. I think it's the right time for the break. We must have the first break now and resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We will continue where we left off. I would just like to see page 1D52, lines 23 to 25, so that the witness can see what Mr. Janc said in his testimony on the 18th of May, 2010. I'm going to quote for the transcript, and, if possible, if we could show that to the witness. We have what Mr. Janc said -- We're now looking at what Mr. Ruez was saying. Can we see what Mr. Janc was saying. Thank you. This is the Bare area. This is what Mr. Ruez was talking about, and those 600 victims. Can we now look at the testimony of Mr. Janc of the 18th of May, 2010. On page 1D52, lines 23 to 25, I asked him the following, I quote: "Do you believe --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we would like to receive the correct page. I think we are now looking at page 1952 and not 1D52. There is no page 1D52. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1952; this is what I says -- and that's what it said and this is what it says here, 1952, line 23: "Do you consider that all the people buried -- the bodies buried in mass graves were, in fact, victims who were deprived of their life in an illegal manner? Thank you." And then can we now look at 1953, lines 4 to 6. He says the following: "My position would be the same as Mr. Ruez's, that the people buried at the primary and secondary mass graves were victims of a crime." And then later Mr. Janc said that all were presented as victims of a crime, regardless of how they were killed, whether in battle or out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this, Mr. Keserovic: Were the victims of a crime those victims also who were killed at Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, to avoid confusion, please, you gave a reference to the first two quotations, but not to the last one. I would like to know where I can find a statement of Mr. Janc that they were presented as victims of crime, regardless of how they were killed. Where do you find -- where can we find that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am not going to stand by what I said. Let's disregard what I said. I'm not able to provide you the exact reference. The previous two references are sufficient for me to be able to put this question to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I really would like to remind you to be very careful if you make such an interpretation of testimony of a witness. Sir, do you recall the question of Mr. Tolimir? No, there was no question yet. Please put a question to the witness. No, the question was: "Were the victims of a crime those victims also who were killed at Baljkovica?" That was the question. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know what happened near Baljkovica. If we're thinking about those who were killed in action in the conflict between the forces who were trying to break through and forces that were trying to prevent that, then these are not victims of a crime, but constitute legitimate military targets. If anything else happened, I really don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. I don't want to spend any more time on this matter, since I need to complete my cross-examination. I would like to ask you now to look at D202 in e-court, please. Can we now look at page 15 in the Serbian and page 16 in the English. Actually, page 19 in the Serbian and page 16 in the English. This will be Article 17. Thank you. Now we can hear Article 17. We'll go over it quickly. These are the rules on the authorities of the corps command in peacetime. My question is: Did we work according -- or operate under that rules, in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. All the rules were taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We can see what the Organ for Intelligence Work was doing. I would just like to read the first item. That states -- the first Article of this, which states: "Planning, organising, and directing intelligence and reconnaissance activities in the corps' zone of responsibility." And above that, it says: "The Organ for Intelligence and Reconnaissance Work is responsible for:" And then it goes on to enumerate all the responsibilities of that organ, down to paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show all of that, please, on the screen to the witness so he could see what these responsibilities are, so that I could then put my question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, we can see the rest of the items, listing the responsibility: "Organising the collection, processing, organising the use of intelligence ..." And so on and so forth, all the way to paragraph 12: "Undertaking other work as prescribed by the regulations on intelligence and security of combat activities and the instructions on the organisation of work of the corps command." My question is: The intelligence organ, was it duty-bound to provide the command with any and all information indicating the activities, the intentions, and the plans of the enemy in wartime?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the main area of work of intelligence/security.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My second question on this is this: Intelligence organs, were they just professional organs in each of the commands where they were located of the corps, the Main Staff, the brigade, and so on? Were they just professional organs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were professional organs, expert organs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at page 35 in Serbian, page 30 in English, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see here Article 29 talking about the security organ. We will do the same as the intelligence organ and we'll just briefly go over the main points and read the preamble. The preamble about the work of the security organ: "The security organ is a specialised organ of the command for organising and implementing security measures and undertaking other specialised work in the field of security that is placed under its responsibility by special regulations and is in this regard responsible for:" And then it goes on to list all its responsibilities in 14 paragraphs that you are going to have a look at. And then once you look at what's on this page, we'll move to the next page so that you could see that as well. Now we can move to the following page so that we can look at the other paragraphs, numbering from 5 to 14. I would just like to quote from paragraph 9, and then I would like to put my question to it. Paragraph 9, in the work of the security organ: "Expertly directing security organ and the military police in the corps command and units and in other JNA units in the zone of responsibility, organising, directing and co-ordinating their activities, providing assistance and controlling their work, especially in regard to counter-intelligence work and tasks." In view of these 14 paragraphs, my question to you is this: Security organs, were they professional organs in the commands, and was their primary task, as it states in this paragraph 9 here, counter-intelligence jobs and tasks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was a professional organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at article on the Intelligence Support of the Armed Forces, and in e-court that would be 00672, page 24, Article 14. I repeat, "Intelligence Support of the Armed Forces, Rules." Can we look at page 24, Article 14, please. In English, it's page 18. Thank you. I'm going to quote this article. We will not go through the whole rule. It states: "The intelligence organ of the superior command staff of the armed forces directs and co-ordinates the expert work of the intelligence and reconnaissance organs and reconnaissance units in directly subordinate commands, staffs, and units; provides expert assistance; and controls their overall intelligence and reconnaissance activity."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: This Rule on Intelligence Support of the Armed Forces, are the intelligence organs defined exclusively as expert organs responsible for the assignments and work that I have just read out in Article 14?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is how it is under the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell us whether, in practice, also the commands in the units of the Army of Republika Srpska, the security organs and the intelligence organs, operated pursuant to the manuals and rules? Did they only carry out professional work that was part of their responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the units where I was, and according to what I know, they did carry out professional duties, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at Rule D203 in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you just have used the document 65 ter 672. It's not in evidence yet, although you have used it with another witness earlier in this trial. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely correct, Mr. President. We omitted to ask that it be tendered during the testimony of Colonel Salapura, and now we would like to ask the Chamber to admit this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir and Mr. Gajic, I was informed that the document 65 ter 672 contains 144 [Realtime transcript read in error "244"] pages. It's a lengthy document, and you have used some pages with specific paragraphs. Could you please tell us if you are tendering the whole document or only those parts you have used or a specific chapter with certain paragraphs. I don't know. I was told by the Registrar that the heading -- the title of the document you have uploaded is different from the whole title because it refers only to specific parts of it. Could you please clarify it, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, document 65 ter 672 is originally on the 65 ter list of the OTP, and we would like to tender the entire document. The reasons, I think, are clear to the Defence and to the OTP. First of all, the document regulates an activity that Mr. Tolimir was involved in during the armed conflict. Secondly, this is a rule that was implemented by the intelligence organs during the armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, meaning the Army of Republika Srpska. Of course, there is no time to go through all of the rules with witnesses in the courtroom. That would require a lot of time. But we believe that the authenticity and the application of the rules during war is something that is not being disputed here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, this was not the question. If you are tendering the whole document, the heading should reflect the content. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We have no objection to the whole rule book going in. They're meant -- these rules are meant to be viewed as a whole, and if you find yourself going through this rule book, it may make a reference to some other paragraph you may want to look at, but we should get the right rule book in. And, of course, I'm confused which rule book we're talking about, but we have no objection to the rule books going in in their entireties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just one thing. On page 40, line 23, you said that it had 244 pages. What I have before me amounts to 144 pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is exactly what I said, but it was probably wrongly recorded. No problem. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just realised what you wanted to indicate in your question. The Defence, of course, did not upload its own copy of the manual on intelligence support. We simply relied on what was uploaded by the OTP. So when it says "paragraph 14" and so on in e-court, it probably reflects something that the OTP intended to use with the witness. We simply relied on the entire document in e-court, and the issue is of a technical nature only. We would just kindly ask the OTP to delete a part of the remark that accompanies the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document 65 ter 672 will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 672 shall be assigned Exhibit D248. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we please have D203, page 10 in the Serbian and 11 in the English version, item 23 of the rules. We can see it now in both languages. I wanted to read something from the rule: "An officer of a security organ of a command, unit, institution, or staff of the armed forces provides specialist management for a military police unit. He recommends the use of the military police unit to the senior officer of the command, unit, institution, or staff, and is responsible to him for the state and activity of the unit. In managing the military police unit, the security organ officer under paragraph 1 of this item has the same rights and duties as officers of arms and services of commands, units, institutions and staffs of the armed forces in managing units of the arms and services of those commands, units, institutions, or staffs."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: My Keserovic, did the security organs have any greater power, in terms of managing or command, as compared to other organs of the commands?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall well, I believe this question was put to me already. In any case, security organs enjoyed the same rights and duties as did other officers and organs of commands of other branches and services. The rights were the same. Everyone was accorded the same status.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at D202, then. Page 17 in the Serbian and 14 in the English version. We had that on the screen a moment ago. It is the rules on the corps command authority in peacetime. Page 17 in the Serbian and 14 in the English language, and we should rotate the Serbian page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see item 2.4, "Organs for Branches," Article 14: "Organs for branches are specialist organs of the staff responsible for the combat readiness of corps branch units, and in this regard they shall:" And we have a number of tasks enumerated in items 1 through 16. My question is this: Did the same tasks apply to security organs vis-à-vis military police units; in other words, that they were responsible for their combat readiness and use according to commander's decision?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all of these rules are very similar, and they flow from the same basic documents, that is to say, the Law on Defence, the Law on the Armed Forces that were in place. It is all derived from the legislation. The tasks are the same. The only difference is that they are specific to the service or branch they apply to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In keeping with the provisions of these rules, as well as in keeping with the laws they invoke, did all command organs, including the security organ, have to abide by them, exercising their rights and duties in accordance with the provisions thereof?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone had to work according to the rules, depending on their position and title, as well as depending on their responsibilities that are based on the rules and laws.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Keserovic, for having come here. I apologise for having put so many repetitive questions in relation to the questions of the OTP. I wish you a safe journey back, and may you enjoy a fruitful future, and health to you and your family. Your Honours, this would be all we had of the witness, and I wish to conclude my cross-examination. I would like to thank all of those who assisted us, and I would like to apologise, yet again, for the mistakes I made in the course of the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. McCloskey, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go back to I believe it's D64, the 12 July document that was in the name of General Tolimir. And I have an original here, just if it may be of any help. I'll just wait for the English to come up. And I think it's fairly represented in the screen, too, but it's just always good to have the original. If we could get some help to get that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if General Tolimir would like to see it, or the Chamber, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be given to the witness. You may put questions to him. But before that, Mr. Gajic should have the opportunity to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. We just wanted to have a look at the document since we have not had occasion to see it in its original form.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And while --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be given to the witness. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we can see, as we've gone over it, it says "The Command of the Drina Corps Intelligence Department," and then it lists "Very Urgent" to various groups. And then can we go to the next page. And here we can see where it's from General Tolimir. And the stamps, one we see it as received. I believe it's 2150 hours on the 12th. And then we see a stamp from the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade. And the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade is a brigade from the Drina Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the brigade changed its position. If I recall well, I believe it belonged for a longer period of time to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps than to the Drina Corps, but it is possible that for a while it was part of the Drina Corps. It may have been resubordinated to it specifically for this task, although I'm not certain. I seem to remember that most of the time it was inside the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, but I do not exclude the possibility that it was part of the Drina Corps as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sokolac, Svetozar Andric, part of the Drina Corps for a long time. Does that help refresh your recollection, originally General Krstic's brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't be specific as to these units. If General Andric was the commander, then he was a brigade commander in the Drina Corps. Based on that, one would conclude that it was a Drina Corps unit. I know that he was in the Drina Corps unit. As for Sokolac, it was in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps, in a way. I must repeat that I seem to remember that at a certain point in time the brigade belonged to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. In any case, Svetozar Andric and the brigade he commanded were in the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General, I've made a mistake. That's the Birac Brigade, which is Sokolac. The 2nd Romanija Brigade is Mirko Trivic. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko? I think that brigade was in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's look at who this is addressed to, if we could go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So can you see one of the addresses is the "2.Rmtbr"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So, in any event, it's an addressee. Now, isn't it possible that the explanation for this is that General Tolimir sent this from the Drina Corps Command, that this isn't a pass-on document, that General Tolimir was at Vlasenica and provided this document and so it was sent under his name from where it was sent from, received by the 2nd Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that General Tolimir could have sent a document from any command post because he was an officer of the Main Staff. He was the chief of sector of the Main Staff. In different periods of time, the Main Staff, too, moved location. What was impossible, however, was for him to send it as the chief of the Intelligence Department of the Drina Corps. That could not and should not have been possible. It would be against the rules. He could not have sent it on behalf of the Intelligence Department of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But he could certainly have sent it from the Intelligence Department of the corps, from the -- which would have been the communication unit from Vlasenica?
