utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he could have sent it from any communications hub of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let me see if I can refresh your recollection. The Judge asked you about who the chief of intelligence was for the Drina Corps, and do you remember a Lieutenant-Colonel Svetozar Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I completely forgot about him. I think he was in the Intelligence and Security Department in charge of intelligence. Svetozar Kosoric, yes. I completely forgot about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in the Drina Corps in July 1995, he would have been part of the staff under the chief of staff, correct, where intelligence departments usually are in corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intelligence organs, in principle, could and were, because of the way the commands worked in reaching decisions, connected to the chief of staff. But the general presumption, and we have the department in question here, should not allow for that possibility. I'm not sure that any VRS corps had a separate intelligence and a separate security department. I think the functions were joined up to the level of corps, in terms of intelligence and security. If they had two departments, then it is possible that the chief of the Intelligence Department was with the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll leave that to others. And you'll recall that you did have a chance to look at your interview statement given to Mr. Ruez 12 October 2000? It was a tape-recorded statement. I think we talked briefly about it at the beginning of the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had an opportunity to see the printed version of the transcript concerning Mr. Ruez's interview in 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is -- it's in e-court as 65 ter 7368. Mr. President, this was something I had not planned on using, but this is a new 65 ter number. But based on some testimony which I'll go over, I wanted to ask him a few questions about it, if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The previous document is still in the possession of the witness, I think. It should be given back to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We shouldn't forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And this should be, in B/C/S, e-court page 71, and page 82 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's on the topic that you spent a lot of time with General Tolimir on, and that is what Major Malinic had told you about those prisoners at Nova Kasaba, especially about the lists. And as you'll recall, you told Mr. Ruez about that way back when, and I want to go over some of what you said to Mr. Ruez. And we should see, at line 9 in the English, it says -- Mr. Ruez asked you: "What does he tell you in his reports regarding the events in the vicinity of Nova Kasaba, the 12th, 13th, 14th, 15th ...?" And you say: "I'm not sure if he told me on that occasion, but around that time, during those days, he said that on the part of the Nova Kasaba-Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road we captured a number of soldiers of the 28th Division or the persons from Srebrenica, and then I think that he told me that Colonel Beara ordered that all of them should be gathered in the soccer field in Nova Kasaba. In his assessment, because he didn't count them properly, around 2500 people were gathered. He allegedly, because I didn't check it out, he allegedly started making lists of the arrested persons, but this was stopped by the arrival of General Mladic, who gathered those people up and addressed them. Allegedly, he told them that they would all be evacuated to where they wanted to go, towards Tuzla, because he [sic] supposedly set off for Tuzla. After that, it must have been the 13th. According to Malinic, buses arrived in the area of Nova Kasaba, and that group was driven to Bratunac, and then in a number of places those people were taken over by the troops of the Bratunac Brigade. There, he lost track of them, and I don't know what happened after that." Do you stand by that statement you gave Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that later we made some clarifications. Up until the point when they were transferred to Bratunac, I think that immediately, even when Mr. Ruez was still there, that there was a misunderstanding and that we immediately corrected it, saying that the forces -- they were handed over to the forces in the zone of the Bratunac Brigade. I'm not sure that these were the troops of the Bratunac Brigade. And, secondly, I didn't understand this last part that you quoted. He did not have any information, he lost contact, and that he doesn't know what's happening with the prisoners of war. I don't think I said that every trace of them was lost, just that he didn't know anything about them. But that would be all that I mean to point out to you. And I think if one keeps reading on, everything will be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And it says what you said, that he just lost track of them, not that he lost all trace of them. Okay, then I'll read a bit more. Ruez says: "Did he tell you what he did with the lists of names that he prepared prior to General Mladic arrived to address the prisoners on that soccer field?" And you say: "No, I don't know if I asked him pointedly, but I have never seen it. I think that at one moment either Malinic or someone else said identification documents were taken from those people, not from all of them but from some of them. But later on, they lost track of them and what happened to those documents." Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to that effect. Major Malinic said that some of the persons present -- in any case, I'm not sure whether it was all of them who had been registered or just some, but that from some of them, at least, their IDs were taken. And I don't know what happened to the IDs and such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Ruez goes on and asks you: "What happened to the lists?" And you say in the next line: "I don't know if anyone asked, but he said he started making lists. He had divided them into groups of those he had gathered --", or, "He had registered and those who were waiting to be registered. I don't know what was the ratio between registered and unregistered prisoners, and I don't know what orders he received concerning that list when General Mladic came." And so just to reiterate, he asked you about that, and you said: "I don't know if anyone asked, but he just started making lists." And you don't know of any orders that Malinic received concerning the lists. Nowhere in this statement or in your similar evidence in the trial where you testified in the Blagojevic case do you mention Malinic receiving an order from Beara to make lists. So is that correct; is it the first time in this trial that you're telling us that Beara is -- ordered Malinic to make lists?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the following line of the document that Mr. McCloskey is quoting, we can see mention of Colonel Beara. It would be very useful if the lines 19 to 22 could be read out to the witness before he starts answering the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is part of the question of Mr. Ruez to the witness. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Same question, General. And you can, of course, see the whole segment there. But the basic question is: The first time ever you have mentioned Beara ordering or telling Malinic to make lists was in this courtroom; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sitting here, I don't think I can distinguish between these things, and I'm not sure if this is the first time I'm saying this. But I think that in relation to the lists, on every occasion I responded by saying that Malinic had started registering the people and making the lists until he was interrupted by Mladic, and that the football pitch in Nova Kasaba was the location that was determined by Beara. Now, whether I have or have not mentioned that Beara was the one who insisted that the lists be made, I'm not sure. But I found out at some later stage, and this is the information that I have, that Beara was the one who wanted to have the lists made. I cannot really now distinguish between the 2000 -- year 2000 and 2004, and cannot clearly say what came from second-hand knowledge and what was my personal experience. It's very hard for me to answer your question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And if we just -- for General Tolimir, we go down to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUEZ SAYS
utterances.text: "When he received the instructions for the information from Colonel Beara," and that would be Malinic, "was Colonel Beara physically present on the ground at that location or did he communicate these things through other means?" And you answer: "I'm not sure, but I think it was passed to the duty officer at the command post that these means -- through the means of communications or by telephone." And that's basically what you've said in the last day or two, the same thing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then Mr. Ruez says: "Did you have, during these days, any contacts with Colonel Beara?" And you say: "Not until the 19th, in the evening, or the 20th, when he appeared in the command post. I knew -- actually, I was told by General Tolimir that he was in the headquarters of the Drina Corps." Now, if you recall yesterday [sic], I believe you told me that General Tolimir, on the morning of the 17th, had told you Beara was in the zone of the Drina Corps; here you're telling Ruez that he was in the headquarters of the Drina Corps. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think you forgot that yesterday was a Sunday. I'm quite sure that you are referring to last Wednesday or Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That weekend just -- I lost it somewhere. You're absolutely right. It was a -- must have been a Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keserovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that this may be a crucial issue, but it's closer to this being somewhere in the zone of the Drina Corps than -- but it's possible also that I was told that he was in the Command of the Drina Corps, because then my memory may have been more alert than it is now. Whether he was in the command itself, in Vlasenica, or at the forward command post, I don't know, but certainly he was in the zone of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. One last reference to this and we'll go on, but if we could go to, it should be, 74 in the B/C/S and 85 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I hope you can find it in the Serbian, but it begins about a third of the way down the page. It's -- well, it's number 9 in the English. And Mr. Ruez says: "I return to the lists. Do you know if a process of stopping writing these lists was due to a fact that the prisoners were transported to Bratunac, or did General Mladic or Colonel Beara give any order related to the process?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These are, in B/C/S, the lines 13 through 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And your answer is: "Not Beara, but Mladic. I am just trying to say what Malinic told me - no need to write anything, because all of them there are going home. Then he addressed them and interrupted the process." So do you recall Malinic telling you that -- what Mladic told him, No need to write anything because the Muslims are going home?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's exactly how he put it, There's no need to write it down. And that's what he told them when he addressed them, There's no need to make lists because you'll be going home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to go to a section of your cross-examination. It was, in fact, right in the beginning of your cross-examination by General Tolimir. It begins --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you have used the OTP statement of the witness. Are you tendering it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think, given this situation, yes, I would. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7368 shall be assigned Exhibit P2221. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you'll recall that he started asking you about your stay together with Colonel Jankovic. This begins at page 13995. And General Tolimir says: "Was everyone in the administration aware of the fact that Jankovic was there only to interpret and that he was summoned to Srebrenica precisely for that purpose; namely, just to be an interpreter?" He goes on and suggests to you that he was just a translator of documents at times and that his assignments there were related to UNPROFOR and ICRC as an interpreter. And you agreed with him. Have you seen the now famous video of General Mladic and Radoslav Jankovic trying to interpret for the Dutch Battalion commander Karremans and his staff at the Hotel Fontana on the 11th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that while responding to a question by Mr. Tolimir I don't think I agreed that Jankovic was only an interpreter. If I remember correctly, I said that I could not identify what his exact task was but that he was used as an interpreter. And as for the footage of General Mladic in Hotel Fontana, no, I didn't have an opportunity to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, what you said to General Tolimir when he suggested that to you, which is -- I'm responding to his suggestion as much as your answer, was, you said: "I was aware that Jankovic was used as an interpreter, and that is why I was not aware what his precise role was within the Intelligence Administration besides that." And then he goes on. Well, General, I want to ask you, since you were there on the 17th and met with Jankovic, if you know of some other duties he was involved in that I suggest were not related to being an interpreter. And if we could go to P554B. Sorry, I'm told it's not on my list. It should have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This should not be broadcast. It's a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, General, this is an intercept the Muslims took. It's dated 17 July, at about 2055 hours. Were you back at the Main Staff by then on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Most probably I was on my way to the Main Staff, but I was not there yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, just in looking at this, it's between someone they identify as C and someone they identify as T, and J is Colonel Jankovic. And we can see that someone's asking for Colonel Jankovic, and then Jankovic says: "Yes, I'm listening." T says: "Well, Jankovic ..." Jankovic says: "Yes." T says: "Listen here. Miletic said ..." And then Jankovic says: "Yes." T says: "That you should write what you want to do." Jankovic says: "Yes." And T says: "And send it urgently by code to Tolimir ." Jankovic says: "I'm in no position to write, man. I'm calling here, and there is ..." And T says: "Listen to what I'm telling you." Jankovic says: "All right." "And the commander will decide what [sic] Tolimir and send you a ..." They don't make that out. And Jankovic says: "Fine." T says: "Well, all right. Take care, mate." And Jankovic says: "Goodbye."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think you misspoke. The fourth line from the bottom, it should read: "And the commander will decide with Tolimir and send you a ..." And then illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I missed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I believe that the version on the screen in Serbian does not correspond to the version read out by Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you referring to the same sentence, Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the entire text. Mr. Tolimir and myself are trying to find that segment of the intercept but haven't had any success. In the version in Serbian, we see something completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was, indeed, the case. It was the wrong page. Now we have the right page. The second part of this document in B/C/S should be the same as the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, please, if you don't see something I'm saying, let me know and it gets a little late, and we ... so take a look, please, if you could, at that. And it's a simple point. Did you become aware, on the evening of the 17th when you returned to Crna Rijeka, that Colonel Radoslav Jankovic, who you spent a good part of the day with, needed something urgently and that he was told to write it down? Anybody ask you about that or mention that to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember anything in relation to Jankovic and that evening except what involved me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you've testified about that already, so I won't ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to P2168.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While this comes up, the Chamber would like to know a different thing, Mr. McCloskey. Will you call the person you talked about, Malinic, as a witness in this case? I don't have the list with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are trying to and we hope to. That's one of those people that I think we're getting close to reaching a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 2 in the English. And I'm going to leave it, if I could -- well, we could try page 2 in the B/C/S. And if we could go to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now, General, you may have to take my word on this, but do you see those initials at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What are those initials?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an opportunity to see this document. You showed it to me. On the basis of its content, I'd say it's Radoslav Jankovic, but I don't know his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to page 1 of the B/C/S, because while it's in Momir Nikolic's name, it's the same as the handwritten one, and I think it's much easier to read, though I'm not going to ask you to go through the whole document. I just want to ask you about this bottom part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see the first paragraphs is talking about wounded prisoners, and the second part is the -- something to do with the Dutch Battalion, Colonel Karremans, and the third one is Medecins Sans Frontieres - pardon my inability to speak French - MSF.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, are you sure that we have the right page in B/C/S on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- should be -- I'm sorry about the quality. It should be paragraph 3 that we see is that big paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Indeed, yes. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Jankovic says -- it talks about: "Will you please use your influence to see to it that all UN and international organisation transports go via Ljubovija. Otherwise, you'll have difficulties providing them with an escort." And by the way, we see that this is to the Main Staff of the VRS, the Intelligence and Security Sector, as well as to the Drina Corps Intelligence and Security Sector. So what Jankovic -- and then Jankovic goes on, and this is what I want to ask you about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you say Jankovic is telling this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see any reference to Jankovic in this document. It is signed by Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's why I went -- you see, the English side has got those initials, that's "RJ." The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your position is it was drafted by Jankovic and signed by Nikolic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. It was what the witness said, Your Honour. He's seen this before, that the rough draft was done by Jankovic and then when Jankovic took it to be typed up, it got typed up and put in the name of Nikolic. Nikolic testified to that, and that's basically what the witness said, part of. I'm sorry I didn't get you the whole story. I know there's lots of pieces, but I don't think there's any disagreement on that. The initials on the handwritten are "RJ," and this is what Nikolic testified to. And the witness just said what he said about having read the document and thinking it was Jankovic, based on the content, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the end of the day, we hope to be in a position to understand that. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry I didn't make that clear, but we can -- well, we can go back to the -- let's just go back to the last page of the -- let's go to the next page of the B/C/S. That's the last page of the document, which is basically the same content as we see in the English translation and as we see in the document under Momir Nikolic's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps leave it like it is on the screen at the moment, and then please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. That's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, and what I want to ask you about: It says Jankovic is asking the Main Staff: "Will you please tell me what stand to take, in terms of authorisation for evacuation of the international organisation MSF, in fact, how to deal with the so-called local staff? This also applies to the interpreters of the military monitors and UNPROFOR." Do you know what he's talking about when he's asking the Main Staff how to deal with the local staff of MSF?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think here that I'm not sure if I connected the things properly. One side of this document is printed, it's typed, and the other page on the other side is in -- is handwritten. Are the contents the same? Is this allegedly Jankovic's handwriting? Probably it is. Is this the same document or is this two different documents? I'm not quite sure about that that, because when you go back to the first page, then we have the security organ, Momir Nikolic. It's a printed document. What is written here and what Jankovic is asking for, some stand, what I can remember is this: During the evacuation of the prisoners of war or the wounded from the Bratunac Medical Centre, there were problems with the local authorities or the local population, some people from Bratunac, regarding their request that all prisoners of war cannot be evacuated and that there are those among them who allegedly committed crimes earlier. So I think that this could refer to that, what Jankovic is asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, General, do you know, when you were there on the 17th, the entire local population had been shipped out on the 13th and that there were wounded left over? And according to your testimony, you saw ICRC actually take some of those wounded away, leaving some behind. Do you remember that? And the Judge asked you a question -- Judge Nyambe asked you a question about that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not thinking of the local population, the Bosniaks or the Muslims. I'm thinking about the local population in Bratunac, which is Serbian. They didn't go anywhere. As far as I understood Jankovic, they were creating problems relating to the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember that MSF and the military monitors - we'll call them UNMOs here - had local staff who would have been able-bodied Muslim men that were still in the Potocari area on 17 July, when you were there, and on the 18th of July, when this letter goes out asking what to do with them? Do you have any recollection about that? You were in the centre of this, so that's why I'm asking you. And so was Jankovic. And it's not just translations, is why I'm asking this.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As for the evacuation, I said what I knew, how the International Committee of the Red Cross that day, in the afternoon, carried out the evacuation. But as far as I can recall, they did not evacuate everyone. A number of people stayed. And then on the following day or a day or two after that, they were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was Jankovic helping organise that in any way or helping as an interpreter in any way the evacuation of those wounded with ICRC on the 17th that you actually saw?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Jankovic there conversing with that woman, a certain Lucy, and with people around who were discussing things relating to the evacuation. I don't really remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So were those part of his tasks that General Tolimir had talked to you about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that one of the tasks was to stop by the medical centre and just see, to follow the evacuation. I think that was the essence of what he was supposed to or what I was supposed to convey to him. He was just supposed to be there and watch as the evacuation was proceeding, just to follow what was going on. I did not transfer any particular responsibility, nor convey any particular tasks to him in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, General, you're saying it was Jankovic's job just to go watch?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if you could put it like that. In order to see, to know, he had to be in touch with somebody, to talk. I don't know if we can just say "watch" and "observe" without that implying that he was also communicating or in contact with anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So him communicating with Lucy would not be something outside his normal job or task as an intel officer working under Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The mission was there. It had specific assignments. And because he was an officer, he could have an intelligence interest in seeing what was going on, how things were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. One more document to see if this has to do with mere translations or some other kind of work. And if we could go to P383B. And this - I see a note - is under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we need to go to the intercept. It's 19 July. It's now the next day. And we want to go to the one that starts at 1432 hours. I've got page 3 on both English and B/C/S. It's not correct in the B/C/S. Maybe we should go to the next page. Yes, that's -- that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is -- we see at 1432 hours on the 19th, the participants are Jankovic and a Colonel Djurdjic. Can you tell us who Colonel Djurdjic was? Or was there a Colonel Djurdjic at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was a Colonel Djurdjic, but I'm not sure in which sector he was, whether he was in the Morale Sector or at the sector -- actually, the Administration for Co-operation with International Organisations and Foreign Representatives. He was somewhere, but I'm not sure what his job was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, that's part of the record in this case. Does it -- do you -- does it -- can you recollect that he was involved in dealing with international organisations, convoy approvals, and the like?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think he just stated it in his last answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, you got part of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The convoy -- was he involved in convoy material at all? I'm sorry for being repetitive.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of those two -- well, I think that is the sector, but I'm not 100 per cent sure. It's either that Sector for Co-operation, which includes convoys and everything that is part of that co-operation in general contacts with representatives of the international community, or the Sector for Morale, but I think that it's more likely that it was this other Sector for International Organisations and Co-operation with International Representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And let's go through this and see if we can make out what he's doing and get your -- see if you recall this or if you can tell us what kind of task this is that he's doing. We see Djurdjic begins by: "Is this Jankovic?" Jankovic says: "Speaking." I won't repeat all of it. And it goes on: "Is it you?" "Yes, it's me," says Jankovic. Djurdjic says: "We should talk, but I've got to make an effort." Jankovic says: "Okay." And then Djurdjic says: "Regarding what you were asking." And Jankovic says: "Yes." And we'll recall what he was asking in the previous document of the 18th, if it may or may not apply. And Jankovic says: "Yes." And Djurdjic says: "The boss has ordered that they be halted." Jankovic says: "Yes." And the Djurdjic says: "This is what he wrote." Jankovic says: "Yes." "That Kristina Smit, the nurse, can go." Does the name Kristina Smit, a nurse with MSF, ring any bells with you? Does -- do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These names, Daniel O'Brian and Kristina Smit, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, then it goes down and, as you say, it mentions Dan O'Brian. Jankovic says: "Yes." Djurdjic says: "The physician?" Jankovic says: "Yes." Djurdjic: "Can you hear me well?" Jankovic says: "Yes." "Do you hear me well?" "I can hear you." Djurdjic says now: "And only women and children can go. Understand?" And Jankovic says: "And what about those young men?" And Djurdjic says: "Others, no. I don't know. They might require --" It may say "the whole group to go," but it's an unclear sentence. Jankovic says -- it's unclear what he says. And Djurdjic says: "Say again?" And then Jankovic says: "That they will require but they have government's permission for all of them to go." Djurdjic says: "Goddamn it. Can we do this through the girl? I have to ask her to act as a mediator here, and now I'll -- we can't -- we can't -- we're having a one-way conversation." Jankovic says: "Listen." Djurdjic says: "Yes." Jankovic says: "So they have permission from the Koljevic government." "Yes." Can you tell us who the Koljevic government is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there's no error here, there is nothing like that. It didn't exist. Professor Koljevic was a member of the Presidency, one of the vice-presidents of Republika Srpska at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Then it goes on. Jankovic says: "That they can all go, they have a list ." Djurdjic says: "Yes, I know, but here, man, I can see the names of a certain Abdulah Kurtovic, Ibrahim Ibrahimovic ..." Jankovic says: "Yes." And then there's a list of a whole lot of other names. I won't go into all of them. Jankovic says: "Yes." Djurdjic says: "Two, four, six, seven men." Jankovic says: "Yes. They are taking them as local staff, and they have permission from the Koljevic." Djurdjic says: "All right, they have the permission, but you know what the procedure -- you --" Excuse me. Let me start over. "All right, they have the permission, but you know that the procedure you, too, took part in ..." Jankovic says: "Great." Djurdjic says: "Pardon?" Jankovic says: "Great, if that's your position, it's good." Djurdjic says: "The procedure is such, goddamn it, that it should be checked whether those who -- are they able-bodied or older than 60?" Jankovic says: "They are able-bodied." Djurdjic says: "They are?" Jankovic says: "Yes." Djurdjic says: "So that's the procedure. And you saw what you left behind in Bratunac the other day." Jankovic says: "Okay." Djurdjic says: "Am I right?" Jankovic says: "Okay." Djurdjic says: "And they, if they agree, let them go in their vehicles and take those women and children." Jankovic says: "All right." Djurdjic says: "And the little orphan, too, some small kid ..." Then they talk about elderly persons. And it goes on: "Two elderly, let them go. Let the elderly go." "Okay." And then Djurdjic says: "Let the elderly go. And tonight, when Toso arrives, you and him must make sure you consult some more, please." And Jankovic says: "All right, I will. When is Toso coming?" Djurdjic says: "In the early evening." Jankovic says: "Okay." And they'll be in touch. "Cheers." Now, did you discuss, when you were with Jankovic on the 17th of July, the problem with able-bodied local staff -- able-bodied men, the local staff of any international organisation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- or, rather, I don't recall talking about the staff. I know that at the DutchBat base I saw a younger man, an interpreter, who would be around there. I remember just recalling him of the local staff, and at least that's what he said who he was. He was serving juices and coffee and at the same time he said that he was an interpreter. And other than that there was no talk about these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who did this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, it is really time for the second break. But if you have only one question left, you should put it to the witness. Or if you need more time, perhaps after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I do need a little more time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: After the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must take our second break and resume at 20 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, before we continue, could you tell us how many more minutes or hours you will use with the witness in re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I will finish by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's no chance to start with the next witness, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, and we had Mr. Janc as a potential gap-filler, but -- and I've spoken to Mr. Gajic, so I think -- we think it's probably best we'll just start with General Milovanovic first thing tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, you had mentioned there was one of the local staff was serving you, I believe. Do you know who that person was working for?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't in the local command, but in the DutchBat Command as local staff. Probably he was working there. He was from Srebrenica, and they probably gave him a job as an interpreter. That's what I understood, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge of General Tolimir, in those days -- on the 19th, as is suggesting in this intercept, of Tolimir helping Jankovic sort out the issue of whether or not the able-bodied men of MSF would be kept or would be let go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd offer -- well, this is already in evidence. So one more document on this topic, 65 ter 2230. And, Mr. President, this topic is not on my list. It was on my Salapura list. I didn't get to it. And with the cross-examination on this topic, I didn't transfer it to my re-direct list. I apologise about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, sir, we see this is a document in B/C/S, and I think we can keep it in B/C/S, but it's just a list of names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, it's under seal. It should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's an MSF document. It's a list of names, and you'll agree with me that these are Muslim names. And if we could just go to the end, the last page. It should be page 5. We can see that the names "Daniel O'Brien" and "Christine Schmitz." Those are the two names that were mentioned in that last intercept we saw?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just to save some time, I can tell you that the name -- the Muslim names on this list are the same names that are in that intercept, so I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you have a translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You know, we've never done an English translation because -- well, we'll ask for one, though. It sort of speaks for itself, but it would be a good idea to have an English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, it will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 2230 shall be Exhibit P2222, under seal. Thank you. Marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, lastly, on this same topic of you and Mr. Jankovic dealing with ICRC on the 17th, could we have 65 ter 507. And, General, I just -- we can see that this is an ICRC press release called "Communication to the Press," dated 18 July, and it talks about -- you can see that it's entitled "ICRC evacuates 88 wounded from Bratunac and Potocari." And just in that first paragraph, it says that: "Three medical teams of the International Committee of the Red Cross, coming from Pale, Bijeljina, and Belgrade, evacuated 88 wounded people from Bratunac and Potocari on 17th and 18th July." Given that you were in Potocari, do you -- does this appear to be some of the people that you witnessed ICRC evacuate on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that those who were at the Bratunac Medical Centre perhaps -- I don't know about Potocari, but I think at least half of these people are those who were in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the last paragraph says that: "The ICRC is also concerned about the fate of thousands of people whose families, displaced to Tuzla, have lost all track of them. It's requesting from the highest Bosnian Serb authorities to give access to all persons captured during the latest events in Srebrenica." Do you remember that by the 18th of July there were press reports like this of thousands of people missing from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that at all. I don't think that thousands were mentioned. I'm not sure when was the first time that I heard about it. At that time, though, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 507 shall be assigned Exhibit P2223. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And just for the record, the previous document is P2222. It was not recorded. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, you'll recall that when -- that Judge Fluegge asked you about when General Krstic became commander of the Drina Corps, and if -- and you mentioned that there should be some documents about that, I think something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there should be an official order appointing him the corps commander. However, I believe that you or someone else showed me an order of the 13th, signed by General Krstic as commander. Given that I couldn't be specific on the issue, I think somewhere -- it's sometime when the operation began, General Krstic was appointed commander. I believe a few days later he was made commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And, Mr. President, I've got a couple of documents on that point. If I could go into those with him just to help clarify your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can we have 65 ter 729.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, take your time to take a look at this. I don't know if it's something anyone has shown you. But we see that it's from the Command of the Drina Corps, dated 13 July, entitled "Hand-over of Corps Commander Duties." And it's in the name of the chief of the Personnel and Legal Affairs, Lieutenant-Colonel Radenko Jovicic, and we see it's send out to several brigades, including the 2nd Romania Motorised Brigade, from our previous questions. And we see that it says: "Pursuant to the decree of the president of the Republika Srpska, in the presence of the VRS Main Staff commander, Colonel Ratko Mladic, the hand-over of duties of the Drina Corps was carried out on 13 July ..." And what does this indicate to you, this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document tells me that as of the moment when, in the presence of General Mladic, the hand-over took place on the 13th of May [as interpreted], General Krstic became commander of the Drina Corps, and that before him it was General Zivanovic who was the commander. This includes all rights and duties that people in such a position have to abide by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We were told that you said the 13th of May. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see we have a -- it looks like a received stamp. I don't see anywhere that we can tell what unit received it. Do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not here. This is a standard stamp. Perhaps someone would be able to identify the signature, but I don't know the codes of the officers in this unit. Therefore, I'm unable to tell you who this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear the account that after General Mladic left the area of Nova Kasaba he went towards the Crna Rijeka but stopped by the Vlasenica headquarters and that afternoon/evening had a brief hand-over of command to General Krstic? Have you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am not familiar with any details pertaining to the hand-over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And could we offer this into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 729 shall be assigned Exhibit P2224. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go to I believe it's 65 ter 1601. Sorry, it's P1601. And we can see that this is from the Drina Corps Command on the 13th of July. It's a regular combat report to the Main Staff of the VRS. Could we go to the next page in both documents. I'm sorry, can we go to -- it's a little longer than I thought. Could we go to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, we can see that this combat report is under the name of Commander Major General Radislav Krstic, and we see a received stamp at 1945 hours. Can we conclude anything from this -- from this document, based how it is -- how it's signed off on, especially if we take into account the previous personnel document that we saw that went out or was received to somebody by around 8.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see from both things that for at least a few hours before that, Krstic was the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, just a final topic and something that General Tolimir spent a bit of time with you on. He started at page 14064, and he said to you: "Since you went through various levels of command within the army, the brigade, the corps, always in the military police, could you tell us, did the police forces have chemical agents for suppressing rebellion or unrest, and did the military police at all levels have such chemical abilities?" And then you said: "At certain levels in battalions of military police there were units, organisational units of company strength that were called anti-terrorist companies. These companies had at their disposal so-called action chemical agents in packages that were ready-made for manual use, mostly it was tear-gas, and occasionally there would be a special rifle available for a bullet that was -- that included tear-gas. So in some units, and this is the legacy of the JNA, the military police had means for chemical activity." Now, when you say "these companies had at their disposal ... for manual use, mostly it was tear-gas," what else did they have besides tear-gas, then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at the very beginning of the sentence there's something wrong. I don't think I mentioned agents, but assets. There was also a rifle, the Sermolji [phoen] type, that the units were equipped with; at least most of them. In any case, these are assets used to incapacitate people momentarily. These are not, as was just said, active chemical agents in the sense of poisonous gasses to be used in combat. These are merely used for incapacitation, to blind the person or to affect their breathing apparatus. It is only applied temporarily, used in closed or small spaces. And mostly such assets have tear-gas. I don't know of any other chemical assets as being supplied to those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you said "mostly," which implies that there is something else besides tear-gas.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I probably used the term "mostly" because I use that term too often in my speech. But what I claim is that I only know of active chemical assets charged with tear-gas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You also said: "These are not, as was just said, active chemical agents, in the sense of poisonous gasses to be used in combat." Were these -- what were these tear-gas assets to be used for, then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those assets, the so-called AG and AF assets - I no longer remember their characteristics; I only remember they were called AG and AF - had plastic charges, the so-called AG and AF hand-grenades. They would be thrown. And following their explosion, they would incapacitate the opponent so as to be unable to defend themselves. Due to shock, such a person affected by it would begin vomiting some five to ten minutes later. That's why we refer to them frequently as shock hand-grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So could they be used in combat by the VRS? Was that allowable by the VRS, to use tear-gas in combat?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chemical assets were not used. As for these assets specifically, it was impossible to use them because it is difficult to throw a grenade far by hand. The assets that the military police had could not be used in combat. It wasn't practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned the -- I believe what we would call a rifle-propelled grenade that had -- could be fit with tear-gas. Could that be used in combat?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am pretty certain I did not mention any rifle-propelled grenades or assets used to fire them. I only referred to a type of bullet, which I believe was less than 20 millimetres, that was filled with tear-gas. One needed the Sermolji rifle to fire it. We see that every day when the police use it in riot control, but this is only at short distances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And General Tolimir read to you a section, on page 14065, item 36 of the Rules of the SFRY: "The military police may use other means of coercion, (chemical means) for temporary incapacitation, special vehicles, devices for forcibly halting vehicles) only in extraordinary cases, upon an authorisation by a commander of the army and other high-ranking military officers." Were you aware of the use of tear-gas hand-grenades and tear-gas bullets, as you call them, to be used against Muslim soldiers hiding out in deep ravines or caves or hidden in buildings or other places, especially in the Zepa operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with any such use of those assets. I'm also completely ignorant of the Zepa operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would it be appropriate, militarily, to use that kind of tear-gas weapon against the Muslim army in that situation, to flush them out of a hiding place, to destroy them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that certain chemical substances are prohibited under the Geneva Conventions, in terms of humane warfare. I cannot say with any certainty whether the plain tear-gas belongs to that category. In general, chemical assets are not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you answer my question: Can you use tear-gas to flush out the enemy to kill them, in the VRS in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I don't think it can be used. Before that, I was the commander of an MP battalion, and I never received such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to 65 ter 7333. It should be e-court page 1 in the B/C/S and 1 in the English. And this is a JNA manual on the use of these sorts of weapons, Mr. President, that I'd like -- given the questions that General Tolimir asked and the answers he got, I'd like to ask this witness about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If you could take a look at that first page, it says: "Special hand-grenades M79 ..." Is that the kind of hand-grenades you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: AF and AG, that was the designation for such hand-grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And so we see here that this is a JNA book on how to use this material, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And it says: "Special hand-grenades M79 ..." And then several numbers I won't go into that are in parentheses. "... and chemical hand-grenades with tear-gas or psychochemical agent, intended for temporary incapacitation of people." Then it says: "Special hand-grenades of AF type are explosive, while those of the AG type are pyrotechnical hand-grenades. Grenades bearing the mark 1 have CS tear-gas charge, and those bearing the mark 2 are charged with a psychochemical agent BZ." What is a psychochemical agent BZ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you paid attention when reading, you realise that this rule was back from 1979. I never had occasion to see AF-2 or AG-2 during my entire career. I only saw AF-1s and AG-1s. Hence, I cannot comment on them. Otherwise, I don't even remember having read this rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to page 13 in English and page 12 in the B/C/S. It's the chapter entitled "Use."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And here we can see that the training for these includes many things that don't have to do with riot control; neutralising resistance at small distances, forcing movement of persons in hiding, and: "Therefore, it is most suited for: Searching the terrain; ambushes; surrounding, destroying (capturing) ..." I won't go through all of this, but it mentions "surrounding" and "destroying" many times in how to use this; throwing it into buildings, using it on terrain. And since the tear-gas, itself, doesn't destroy anyone, what is anticipated here? How does a person get destroyed when tear-gas is used against them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One would conclude from this that if used in combat, in subsequent action, such personnel is destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to offer this book into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please indicate how many pages it contains?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told 27 pages, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think so. Some of it is this BZ agent, which, for Your Honours' knowledge, is this psychochemical agent, that the witness doesn't know about, is not part of this case. We don't see that being sent to the Rogatica Brigade. You'll remember what we did see, those were the tear-gas grenades and rifle grenades, just for your memory. But I would have that whole book so you can see it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we go back to the first page to see the date again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We need to blow it up to see the "1988." I think you'll see it. The -- can you put the star, please -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, that's a -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It will be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7333 shall be assigned Exhibit P2225. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Witness, General, I just have a very simple clarification question. If I understood correctly, you said, on page 83 of the transcript, that you have never seen this instruction before on the use of these weapons, but I see that the manual was written in 1981 and you had your training at the JNA, so I'm wondering how -- did you just say correctly that you had never seen this book during the entire -- during your entire career?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I completed the Military Academy in 1981, specialising in armoured units. During my training at the academy, I had no occasion to see these assets. As for units of the military police, I joined them for the first time in 1990, when I was appointed deputy battalion commander. As of that moment on, until the beginning of the war, I became acquainted with most of the assets. As for any individual assets, I never studied each and every one. I did read some general rules, but I never attended such specialised training for military policemen at lower level. My first position in the military police was deputy commander of the Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just a couple more things we should be able to finish up. Could we see 65 ter 7335, and this is a -- this is another document on the same topic, Your Honour, that is in direct response to this issue brought up by the general. It does not have a previous 65 ter, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Defence objects to the use of this document, since this is something from 2005 and we are addressing events from 1995. As lawyers, I believe this objection is sufficiently clear, and I am reluctant to elaborate any further in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is -- he was asked about the Geneva Conventions and the use of this material, as far as I recollect, and so I think I'm free to ask him about the ICRC's view on this material, be it 1995 or later. This has been a developing area in military rules and regulations since the Conventions of the 19 -- well, before the 1940s.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How can the answer of the witness be helpful to assess the position of the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The question would merely be: Are you aware of the ICRC's views on the use of riot-control agents in warfare?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You could put this question to the witness without showing this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I very well could, but I know someone would ask me to back up where I'm coming from. But that's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, of course, the question is legitimate; however, it ought to be limited to 1995. Law cannot be applied retroactively. Something created after 1995 is something we cannot rely on in these proceedings, and there is no need to analyse it in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me be clear. This is not the law. This is just the ICRC's view of the law on a very interesting and complicated area at times. And I'll get to this -- it won't take long at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I see you're still on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is certainly an interesting issue. But if we consider this document, I believe we need much more time, since it entails a number of explanations. The document was not translated, and we would probably have to read out at least two or three paragraphs if we want to rely on it in a fashion appropriate. It refers to what countries agreed to it and when the assets in question were used and when they were not used. It is a rather complicated legal matter. I'm reluctant to put our position before the witness so as not to be accused of instructing him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't -- in the sake of time, I don't need to use this now. I'll go to the next document, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But you should come to an end. We are running out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just had five minutes taken away, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could: Sir, you've talked about the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, it is five minutes past 7.00. We are really running out of time. I have no idea -- there's still a list of documents to be used in re-direct. How much time do you need for completion of your re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a couple of minutes. This really was meant to be my last -- last two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Very few minutes. Please continue and conclude as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of the protocol for the prohibition of the use of asphyxiating and poisonous and other gasses and of bacteriological methods of warfare of the Geneva -- from 17 June 1925 of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The whole Army of Republika Srpska was aware of the ban on the use of poisonous agents in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was BC -- BZ, excuse me, as we just saw described in that book from the 1980s, one of those banned chemical agents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what "BZ" stands for. I have tried to remember. I don't know what sort of a charge this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you aware that the ICRC felt that tear-gas should be one of the banned -- one of the banned materials from the 1925 Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I knew that. But since tear-gas was permitted for use even in peacetime for us, I'm not sure that I knew that there was a general ban on its use.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes now your examination and your testimony in this case. Thank you very much that you were able to come to The Hague and to provide us with your knowledge and recollection. Now you are free to return to your normal activities. Thank you very much again. We have to adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow at 9.00 in Courtroom III. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of May, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.08 p.m.,
